why_this_persona: Anna is the only one of the three who has to explain this to other people: her file carries the interest line about understanding AI well enough to explain it to the team and the owner, her 2026 goal says 'adopt AI' while an IT memo says no client data, and the source reel's own worked example is a company-document question, "where's my company's IT desk?", which is a version of the question she answers twenty times a day.
interest: How AI works: How AI actually works, enough to explain it to the team and the owner
question: I am the one who has to explain this to the team and to the owner, and I cannot say in my own words what it knows about us and what it does not. What do I put in front of them at the next meeting?

borrow.hook_logic: Compress a subject the viewer is afraid of into one sitting and promise your own method for it, not a syllabus. The source does it in the first 4.2 seconds: 'If you had to learn the fundamentals of AI in one day, here's how I do it' (beat 0). We keep the compression and cut the scale down: not nine words in one day, one question in ten minutes. The source spends its opening on the speaker's method, which is the weaker half of I-06; ours spends it on the screen doing the thing, per I-05 and I-09.
borrow.proof_mechanism: A contrasting pair of questions, one the machine can answer and one it cannot, with the second one being about the viewer's own company. The source builds the whole lesson on it: 'how big is Central Park' against "where's my company's IT desk?", and the fix is handing over the company documents (beat 3), then a one-line callback that closes the term (beat 4). We keep the pair and stop telling it. The second question is asked on our own screen, against our own internal document, and the guess is left visible before the page is attached.
borrow.ordering: Hook, the plain definition, the mechanism as one everyday picture, a callback that tells the viewer they have actually learned something, then a re-hook that names what is still missing, then how it was made and what it cost (beats 0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6). The re-hook at 37.8 s is the rare part worth taking: only 15 of 264 reels in the corpus have an explicit one (I-26), and it is what holds the second half of a 58-second reel together.
borrow.visual_grammar: Text-before-picture escalation on a static talking head: pink keyword tags appear one at a time around her face and the density climbs low to medium to high across scenes 0, 1 and 2, so the subject grows while the shot never changes. A full-bleed illustrative photo carries the scale half of the contrast pair (scene 5, aerial Central Park). We keep the one-line-at-a-time escalation and drop the floating glossary, because the nine words are the thing we are refusing to teach. We do not copy scene 4's split screen over facecam (I-10: the most-used opening in the niche and the weakest); the lesson page becomes a full-frame insert, arranged screen, face, screen per I-09 and I-11.

change.process: The staff question answered out of the company's own handbook, in a 40-person services company: somebody asks how much notice they need to give for leave, which form a client signature goes on, what the client-data rule actually says. Today it is answered from Anna's memory or by hunting for the file, which is why 'where is this file' reaches her twenty times a day. Owner is Anna: the handbook, onboarding and the processes are in her job description and nobody else's.
change.friction: Anna is the source of truth and the bottleneck at the same time, and she has no words of her own for the thing she is being measured on. She is evaluated on AI adoption while an IT memo forbids client data, so the only safe place to start is the company's own internal documents, and nobody has told her that. When the owner runs her proposals through a chat and sends back a wall of text, she cannot say why his answer is worse than hers, because the vocabulary belongs to the vendors who sent the decks. The Copilot licence the company already pays for sits there with no training behind it.
change.ai_boundary: The machine reads the handbook page and quotes it, and says which page and which date it read. It never answers a policy question out of its own knowledge: where the handbook is silent, the answer is 'not in the handbook' and the question comes to Anna. Anything about a named person, hiring, performance or an HR case stays with a person, which is already on Anna's list of jobs that should never be handed over. Nothing a client owns goes in: the source document is the company's own handbook, and this is the one first use that does not touch the memo. Nobody's hours are being replaced; Anna is getting hers back.
change.next_action: Take the one question your team asks you every week. Find the paragraph in your own handbook that answers it, put a name and a review date at the top of that page, then ask the chat the same question twice, once with the page attached and once without, and read the two answers side by side.

hook: Your team can understand AI in one question: ask it something only your own handbook knows, and watch it answer confidently and wrong.

on_screen.opening_screen: Our own internal rule typed into a chat with nothing attached: 'how many days are there between the plan and the publication?' and the confident wrong answer filling the frame, caption already burned in, no face (I-09, I-05). The real answer is three to seven days and it is in RULES.md section 2, which the chat has never seen. Second screen, same question with that page attached, and the answer quoting the line.
on_screen.human_check: The source document open beside the answer with an owner's name and a review date in its header, kept outside the chat. On screen with it, the list of test questions we asked before trusting it, and the ones it got wrong. Where the document is silent the reply is 'not in the handbook', routed to Anna, never an invented policy.
on_screen.cost_line: First place to look is the Copilot licence the company already pays for, which adds nothing to the monthly bill; Anna's own ceiling before she has to ask the owner is $20 a month. It stops paying the day somebody has to maintain a second copy of the handbook to keep it working, and at $100 a month with nobody counting hours back this audience says no.

claims.text: 283 515 plays against this author's median of 19 624, robust_z 1.77, with 58.1 saves and 17.8 shares per thousand plays: the highest save rate in the batch.
The reel completes one full teaching unit on screen instead of promising one after the CTA, which is the reason ta-v1 gives for that save rate: the viewer saves a thing that already worked on them.
The source's own worked example of a question the machine cannot answer is a question about the company: "where's my company's IT desk?", fixed by handing over the company documents.

Hooks that show a result or a running artefact first run at median robust_z 2.17 and view_lift 5.81 against 1.21 and 1.80 for every other hook type, the largest hook effect measured, which is why the wrong answer is on screen before anyone speaks.
Opening on a screen rather than a face carries median share_rate 0.0213 against 0.0140 across the 35 reels that do it, creator-normalised +0.285.

Split screen is the most-used opening in the niche, 73 of 266 reels, and the weakest, median robust_z 1.03 against 1.43, so the source's lesson-page-over-facecam scene is rebuilt as a full-frame insert.
Only 15 of 264 reels contain an explicit re-hook beat, and this one has it at 37.8 s, which is the structural part worth borrowing for a reel this long.

The corpus names a developer audience in 54 of 266 reels and a non-technical operator in only a handful, and the evidence recommends the builder register over the educator register, which is why we run one question instead of defining a term.
Reels whose stated desire is a ready-made artefact carry median save_rate 0.0346 against 0.0270 for the rest, and the save comes from there being something to collect rather than from gating it.
Trust is the second-largest request in the audience pass, 35 of 101 threads, and the answer to an owner checking your work against a chat is to give the same chat the sources, 69 votes in r/msp.
Anna's cost ceiling is $20 a month before she asks the owner, she uses what the company already pays for, and she needs a monthly number and hours back before asking for budget.

The two screens the shoot opens on: the same internal question answered without the page and with it, with a count of how many of our test questions were answered from the document and how many were guessed.

notes: The batch gives no format_slot and no radar_facts for this code, so the slot is chosen here. Teardown over Radar: the source's subject is a free learning site and a list of nine terms, there is no tool or model whose arrival changes Anna's week, and a list of terms with no exit to a process is the disqualifier in RULES.md section 2. Teardown over Builds: we have not built or broken anything here yet, the ten-question run against our own documents is PLANNED, and Builds without something that broke is an advert. Both Teardown gates are met: a concrete process with a named owner (the staff question answered from the handbook Anna owns) and a reason to forward (the same question asked twice, one confident wrong answer and one quoted from the page, with one document as the entire difference). The routing hint pointed at Anna, correctly, but on the wrong line: it scored 1.18 on the word 'documents' and reached for her client-document routing interest, while the reel's subject is understanding, not a filing flow. Emma scored 0.59 on the word 'website' alone. Rick also has 'What AI actually is, in plain words, without the hype', and he is the near miss; the tiebreak is that he has nobody to explain it to and his file says he judges by whether the job is done right the first time, while the explaining job is in Anna's line verbatim. The process the card is proved on is her other line, 'Policy questions from staff answered from one source document with an owner and a date', which is the same mechanism the source teaches with Bob. Dropped from the source on purpose: the nine-term glossary, because the words are what this audience is not asking for ('what is AI' appears 5 times in 101 threads and never from an owner in those words), and the whole proof beat that sells the build tool's free mode, because 'free' is not an answer for this audience when the bill arrives later (RULES.md section 11.2.2). No comment ask: the artefact that fits this interest is the 'ask it again with sources' reply template on Anna's list, and it does not exist in artefacts/ yet. If it is written before the shoot, the ask becomes comment SOURCES; until then the card ends on the next action and the page is published rather than gated (I-29). ASR in the source renders Replit as 'Raplit'; irrelevant to us since the tool is dropped.
